entries.title: Moon, Venus and Spica Meet
entries.explanation: Not all those who wander are lost. A night sky example is that planets wander, and in fact the very word “planet” comes from “wandering star” in Greek. As planets shift relative to fixed stars, they may appear from our perspective to get closer to other astronomical objects. Such meetings are called conjunctions. They don’t happen by chance, but follow the precise laws of celestial mechanics. This peaceful image, captured in Poland, shows the crescent Moon above the Tatra Mountains, and bright Venus close by, a little lower in the horizon. The bright star to the left of Venus is Spica in the constellation of Virgo, the Maiden. Spica is one of the brightest stars in the sky, only about 250 light-years away. It was found in 1890 that Spica is a binary star: two massive blue stars orbiting each other every 4 days. But earlier this year it was reported that Spica, the current companion of wandering Venus, is actually a triple system. Tomorrow’s picture: what’s next?

entries.title: NGC 206 and the Star Clouds of Andromeda
entries.explanation: The large stellar association cataloged as NGC 206 is nestled within the dusty arms of the neighboring Andromeda galaxy along with the galaxy’s pinkish star-forming regions. Also known as M31, the spiral galaxy is a mere 2.5 million light-years away. NGC 206 is found at the center of this sharp and detailed close-up of the southwestern extent of Andromeda’s disk. The bright, blue stars of NGC 206 indicate its youth. In fact, its youngest massive stars are less than 10 million years old. Much larger than the open or galactic clusters of young stars in the disk of our Milky Way galaxy, NGC 206 spans about 4,000 light-years. That’s comparable in size to the giant stellar nurseries NGC 604 in nearby spiral M33 and the Tarantula Nebula in the Large Magellanic Cloud. Tomorrow’s picture: pixels on the Moon

entries.title: Apollo 12 and Surveyor 3
entries.explanation: Put on your red/blue glasses and gaze across the western Ocean of Storms on the surface of the Moon. The 3D anaglyph shows Apollo 12 astronaut Pete Conrad visiting the Surveyor 3 spacecraft in November of 1969. Surveyor 3 had landed at the site on the inside slope of a small crater about 2 1/2 years earlier in April of 1967. Visible on the horizon beyond the far crater wall, Apollo 12’s Lunar Module Intrepid touched down less than 200 meters (650 feet) away, easy moonwalking distance from the robotic Surveyor spacecraft. This stereo image was carefully created from two separate pictures ( AS12-48-7133, AS12-48-7134 ) captured on the lunar surface. They depict the scene from only slightly different viewpoints, approximating the separation between human eyes. Tomorrow’s picture: meteors through Orion
entries.copyright: Apollo 12, Alan Bean – Stereo Image Copyright: Kevin Frank

entries.title: Leonid Meteors Through Orion
entries.explanation: Where will the next meteor appear? Even during a meteor shower, it is practically impossible to know. Therefore, a good way to enjoy a meteor shower is to find a place where you can sit comfortably and monitor a great expanse of dark sky. And it may be satisfying to share this experience with a friend. The meteor shower depicted was the 2022 Leonids and the view is from Hainan, China looking out over the South China Sea. Meteor streaks captured over a few hours were isolated and added to a foreground image recorded earlier. Leonid meteor streaks trace back to the constellation of Leo and were here seen streaking across the constellation of Orion. The bright red planet Mars appears near the top of the image. The Leonids peak in mid-November every year and so will peak again this week. Bonding over their love of astronomy, the two pictured meteor enthusiasts, shown celebrating their common birthday this month, were later married. Tomorrow’s picture: open space

entries.title: NGC 7129: Star Formation with Jets from Webb
entries.explanation: How do stars form? To help answer this question, NASA used the James Webb Space Telescope to take the featured detailed image of the star-forming region NGC 7129 in infrared light. Star formation progresses when gravity pulls together massive amounts of gas, but soon things can get complicated when previously formed stars emit powerful jets and winds — and some then explode. Opaque dust can form in the cool atmospheres of stars and, when dispersed, can obstruct visible-light images. Many stars can be seen to be forming in the featured image, with the young stars on the left, in the gold-colored gas, typically being more mature than the young stars on the right — in the red region. Jets and wind s likely cause the filamentary nature of the red-colored gas. Studying stars at different stages of development bolsters understanding about what physical processes are most important and when. Tomorrow’s picture: sky duel

entries.title: Milky Way versus Aurora
entries.explanation: Are these two giant arches battling for control of the sky? No, but it sure looks like it! The arch on the left is the central band of our Milky Way Galaxy, an ancient system of stars, gas, and dust that predates our Earth and is very far away. The arch on the right, by contrast, is an auroral ribbon that is only hours old, composed of energized atoms and molecules, and is close by — right in Earth’s upper atmosphere. These chance-superposed titan s have our Sun in common, a stellar member of the Milky Way that ejects energetic particles which create aurora s. Far behind the middle of the auroral arch is the Big Dipper. Even farther in the distance is the Andromeda galaxy — the bright spot near the top of the frame, just left of center. The featured image was taken about a month ago from Kvaløya in northern Norway. Tomorrow’s picture: open space

entries.title: A Medium-Sized Solar Flare
entries.explanation: What a flare for the chromatic! Today’s image combines a series of images taken over ten minutes capturing the Sun ’s chromosphere, the layer of the Sun ’s atmosphere above its surface where the temperature rises. Why would the Sun become hotter farther away from its core? This is potentially due to energy from the swirling magnetic fields extending up through the Sun’s atmosphere. Those same magnetic fields can twist and snap, releasing light and energetic particles as a solar flare. The H-alpha filter used for today’s image captures light from energized hydrogen atoms as they travel off the Sun’s surface during a flare on May 14, 2025. This flare was classified as an M1 based on GOES observations, meaning it was moderately bright in X-rays. M-class flares can cause radio blackouts at Earth’s poles and minor radiation storms that can harm astronauts. They aren’t even the most powerful flares! NASA, NOAA, and other agencies monitor the Sun to predict and identify such storms so we can protect humans on Earth and in space. Tomorrow’s picture: a horse of a different color

entries.title: The Horsehead and Flame Nebulas
entries.explanation: Today’s image could have been a painting. But what do these colors mean? The brightest star, left of the center, is blue Alnitak (the Girdle): a triple star system best known for being the easternmost star in Orion’s Belt. The instantly recognizable shape of a dark horse’s head at the center is the aptly named Horsehead Nebula. It is about five light-years tall and lies approximately 1,500 light-years away. It is made of dust and gas that obscure the red glow behind it, which is caused by hydrogen gas being ionized by the bright star Sigma Orionis at the top. The orange nebula with dark filaments on the left is the Flame Nebula. Closer to the Horsehead, the blue reflection nebula NGC 2023 is actively forming stars. The data for this “painting” were collected for almost six hours at the Utah Desert Remote Observatories, but the equipment was remotely controlled by the astrophotographer from his home, over 2,000 km away in Illinois. Tomorrow’s picture: V-G-R

entries.title: V-G-R
entries.explanation: On November 17, fans of interstellar spaceflight around planet Earth were invited to shine a message into the night sky. Traced by a flashlight beam switched on and off, the dashes and dots of a Morse code message captured in this time exposure from the Emirates Astronomical Observatory are read V-G-R. That’s a call sign for the Voyager 1 spacecraft currently in interstellar space some 26 billion kilometers away. How long did it take the message to reach humanity’s most distant interstellar spacecraft? Traveling at the speed of light, the answer is one day. In fact, the Voyager 1 spacecraft was confirmed to reach its one light-day distance milestone on November 18, at 10:16:07 UTC, nearly 50 years after launch in 1977. For extra credit, fans of math can calculate that at one light-day per 50 years, Voyager 1 will reach its one light-year (365 light-days) distance milestone in about 18,250 years. Tomorrow’s picture: cruising

entries.title: Voyager’s Neptune
entries.explanation: Cruising through the outer solar system, the Voyager 2 spacecraft made its closest approach to Neptune on August 25, 1989, the only spacecraft to visit the most distant ice giant planet. Based on the images recorded during its close encounter and in the following days, this inspired composited scene covers the dim outer planet, largest moon Triton, and faint system of rings. From just beyond Neptune’s orbit, the interplanetary perspective looks back toward the Sun, capturing the planet and Triton as thin sunlit crescents. Cirrus clouds and a dark band circle Neptune’s south polar region, with a cloudy vortex above the pole itself. Parts of the very faint ring system along with the three bright ring arcs were first imaged by Voyager during the fly-by, though the faintest segments are modeled in this composited picture. Spanning 7.5 degrees, the background starfield is composed from sky survey data centered on the constellation Camelopardalis, corresponding to the outbound Voyager’s view of the magnificent Neptunian system. Still cruising in 2026, the Voyager 2 spacecraft is now in interstellar space. Tomorrow’s picture: swirling

entries.title: Swirls and Colors on Jupiter from Juno
entries.explanation: What creates the colors in Jupiter’s clouds? No one is sure. The thick atmosphere of Jupiter is mostly hydrogen and helium, elements which are colorless at the low temperatures of the Jovian cloud tops. Which trace molecules provide the colors remains a topic of research, although small amounts of ammonium hydrosulfide are one leading candidate. What is clear from the featured color-enhanced image — and many similar images — is that lighter clouds are typically higher up than darker ones. Pictured, light clouds swirl around reddish regions toward the lower right, while they appear to cover over some darker domains on the upper right. The featured image was taken by the robotic Juno spacecraft in 2018 during its 14th low pass over Jupiter. Juno continues in its looping elliptical orbit, swooping near the huge planet every 33 days and exploring a slightly different sector each time around. Tomorrow’s picture: emerging darkness

entries.title: The Emergence of Dark Nebula Lynds 1251
entries.explanation: If you stare into space for a long time, what might you see? At first, you might only see the usual brightest stars, but if your eyes (or camera) could continue to collect light, you would see increasingly more. In the direction of the featured image, after only a few minutes, you would begin to notice some regions without stars. As your staring continued, the dark region would become better defined, and after a full 20 hours, you would notice a strange dark structure. To celebrate, you use digital processing to brighten the image and enhance the colors. At the end, you might have an excellent image of Lynds 1251 (LDN 1251), a star -forming region laced with opaque brown-appearing interstellar dust. Also known as the Rotten Fish Nebula, LDN 1251 is home not only to young stars and dust, but also, your long staring indicates, energetic shock waves, fast stellar winds, and powerfully beamed jets. Tomorrow’s picture: galaxies ringing

entries.title: Galaxies Battle in the NGC 7771 Group
entries.explanation: After this galaxy battle, only one galaxy will remain. Already visible in the featured picture are rings and faint star swirls from previous gravitational encounters. Known collectively as the NGC 7771 Group, these galaxies lie almost 200 million light-years away toward the high-flying constellation Pegasus. The largest galaxy, barred spiral NGC 7771 on the lower right, is itself about 75,000 light-years across, and the galaxy on the upper left is spiral NGC 7769, which is almost as large. As these and other smaller galaxies make repeated close passages, they will all likely merge into one very large galaxy. Playing out over billions of years, the merger process is understood to be a normal part of the evolution of galaxies. Studying galaxy clashes like this helps humanity to better understand the possible merger between our own Milky Way and Andromeda galaxies. Tomorrow’s picture: open space

entries.title: SPHEREx Seeing Through Dust
entries.explanation: What is blocking the center of the Milky Way? During its 13 billion years, our Milky Way has collected a lot of dust. In contrast to the skin cells, dirt, pollen, and other debris that make up the dust behind your couch, cosmic dust is hundreds of times smaller and made of tiny compounds of oxygen, carbon, and other elements released into space when a star dies. Today’s video shows infrared light from the Milky Way’s center gathered by NASA’s SPHEREx satellite. Each false color in the video corresponds to the infrared color associated with the wavelength shown in the top left. In the near-infrared, like 1.2 microns, light gets absorbed and scatters off of dust particles. SPHEREx then sees the Galactic Center almost entirely blocked by clouds of dust. In the mid-infrared, though, light is able to pierce through the dust and reach SPHEREx. This is similar to, but not exactly, why sunsets are red! Tomorrow’s picture: a sandy view of the Milky Way
